It sits at 0.0 for the same auxiliaries written with a straight apostrophe ('ve and 'll as single tokens) and for uncontracted have/will, sits at 0.0 for ordinary words that contain the letters ve (government, vegan) and at about 0.5 for the word-initial ' ve' token (id 1569), is weak on the other curly clitics ’s, ’m, ’d, ’t and ’re (0.2–0.6 in a short sentence, up to about 1.1 after a full preceding clause, versus 1.3–3.3 for ’ve/’ll), and only a few standalone words (happen, meant, capable, truly) reach 1.0–1.8 in some sentences.

adversarial_test_results.detail: Same review-of-3D-TVs topic and near-identical wording to the top examples, but the contractions use the straight apostrophe, which tokenizes as the single token 've (no bare ve, no apostrophe bytes) and which the hypothesis says leaves the pole at 0.0.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: I've read every report you've sent, and you've done fine work.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Straight-apostrophe I've/you've in ordinary prose, predicted 0.0 because the tokenizer produces only single 've tokens, with no bare 've' continuation token and no apostrophe byte tokens.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: We have examined all the evidence and we will present our findings on Thursday.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Uncontracted 'have'/'will', the hypothesis's explicit 0.0 case since neither the clitic token nor the curly-apostrophe bytes occur.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Government regulators said the vegan restaurant had violated the noise ordinance.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Ordinary words containing the letters 've' (Government and vegan tokenize as whole words), which the hypothesis says score 0.0 without a standalone 've' token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The shop’s display looked fine, and the owner’s dog slept by the door.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Curly ’s possessives, which tokenize as two apostrophe byte tokens plus a bare 's' in one short sentence, one of the other curly clitics the hypothesis rates only 0.2–0.6, far below its 1.3–3.3 ’ve/’ll peak.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: I’m certain I’m not the only one who noticed.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Curly ’m contractions, tokenized as two apostrophe byte tokens plus a bare 'm' in a short sentence, predicted 0.2–0.6 and inactive because the peak clitic is 've', not 'm'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They’d rather we’re early, so we can’t miss the start.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Three other curly clitics (’d, ’re, ’t) packed into one short sentence, each tokenized as the apostrophe byte pair followed by bare d/re/t, all predicted weak at 0.2–0.6.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He said ‘we will go’ and left the room without another word.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Curly quotation marks put the apostrophe byte tokens in the text with no ’ve/’ll clitic after them (the closing ’ is followed directly by ' and'), so the hypothesis predicts only the weak 0.2–0.6 behaviour it reports for byte tokens followed by other continuations.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: In phonetics class we learned that ve is a rare syllable in some dialects.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The checked tokens include the word-initial ' ve' token (id 1569), which the hypothesis rates at only about 0.5, so this should stay below the ’ve/’ll peak.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Y’all should meet ma’am at the gate before noon.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Curly apostrophes in y’all/ma’am produce the same apostrophe byte pair but the wrong continuations (bare all/am instead of ve/ll), which the hypothesis predicts is weak like the other non-’ve curly clitics.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They’ve rebuilt the engine twice since the accident.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Checked tokens are They | byte | byte | ve, the exact pattern claimed, so the hypothesis predicts a 1.3–2.5 peak on the bare 've' continuation token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He’ll send the invoice once the parts come in.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Checked tokens are He | byte | byte | ll, the exact pattern claimed, so the hypothesis predicts a 1.2–2.3 peak on the bare 'll' continuation token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The officers who’ve reviewed the footage say the van ran the light.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Checked tokens are who | byte | byte | ve in a relative clause in a news/court register, a novel context that the tokenizer-level hypothesis says should still fire on the bare 've' token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: # I’ve already restarted the service; next time we’ll capture the logs first.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Checked tokens contain both I | byte | byte | ve and we | byte | byte | ll inside a code comment, an unusual position the tokenizer-level hypothesis says should still fire on the bare clitic tokens.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The lighthouse at Cranby Point had stood through a century of storms, but by the spring of its hundredth year the iron stair had rusted through in a dozen places and the lantern room leaked whenever the wind came off the sea. A committee of local residents raised the money for repairs, and the county council matched the largest single donation from the harbour trust. Work began in the second week of April, after the last of the winter gales had passed and the road down to the point was dry enough for the trucks. The crew stripped the old paint back to bare metal, replaced the spiral stair section by section, and rebuilt the lantern gallery with galvanised steel, working from a scaffold that swayed in every gust off the water.

The surveyor came out twice a week and left notes in a ledger that the archivist later transcribed into the parish records. Every delay was written down, every delivery logged, and there were plenty of both: a shipment of glass panes arrived cracked, the crane hire was cancelled because the driver was ill, and a week of fog kept the boat away with the last of the brass fittings. The foreman kept a running list of tools on the back of a cigarette packet, and lost it at least twice. Local children brought sandwiches to the men at lunchtime, and someone hung a kettle in the keeper's cottage, though the electricity had been cut off years before.

By the middle of June the glass was in and the lantern tested, and the old lamp was replaced with a modern light that could be serviced from a small platform instead of the gallery itself. A retired engineer from the neighbouring village volunteered to check the wiring, and his report is still pinned to the wall of the cottage. The committee held a small party on the shingle below the tower, and the oldest resident, who remembered the last full repaint in 1948, cut a ribbon across the door with a pair of borrowed shears. Photographs were taken for the parish magazine, and the story of the repairs ran for half a page in the county paper. In the last of the light, after most of the visitors had gone home, the keeper climbed the new stair for the first time and stood in the lantern room where the lamp turned and turned above the water. Three summers of fundraising, two hundred letters, and a great deal of bad weather later, we’ve finally got the old tower back in working order, and the light still sweeps across the bay every night as it did a hundred years ago.
